description: Interactive videogame for "Fenómeno del niño" and the impact in Piura
summary:
Pacha Ñawi is an educational video game that turns Earth science data into accessible investigations. We developed two cases from Peru’s Piura River basin during the 2016–2017 episode: precipitation estimated by NASA GPM IMERG and root-zone soil wetness modeled by NASA MERRA-2, accessed through NASA POWER. Each case includes 115 daily records, supported by contextual reports from SENAMHI and ENFEN.
Players first learn what each variable measures, inspect evidence cards and charts, and classify the trend as “Significant” or “Not significant.” Four progressive levels introduce the p-value, Sen’s slope, temporal autocorrelation, and the limits of scientific inference. Reproducible Python scripts perform all scientific processing beforehand; the game presents the prepared results without running statistical analyses during play.
Our project addresses Pacha ñawi by connecting NASA data with an engaging, locally relevant learning experience. It aims to strengthen scientific literacy and help university students distinguish statistical significance, change magnitude, and causal claims. An integrated manual, complete datasets, and reproducible analyses support classroom use and further exploration.
details: Pacha Ñawi is a Spanish and English language educational desktop game that introduces university students to the interpretation of environmental time series. Players work with evidence cards, scientific charts, and an integrated manual. The experience focuses on two real-data cases, without fictional characters. The first case examines daily precipitation estimated by NASA GPM IMERG. The second examines root-zone soil wetness modeled by NASA MERRA-2. Both datasets were accessed through NASA POWER and cover December 1, 2016, through March 25, 2017: 115 consecutive daily records for the Piura River basin in Peru. Reports from SENAMHI and ENFEN provide historical and environmental context; the numerical series used in the statistical tests come from NASA. Before entering the game, the data are processed into basin averages using weights based on the area of intersection between each grid cell and the basin. The workflow checks dates, missing values, spatial coverage, and valid ranges. It uses 120 intersecting cells for precipitation and 10 for soil wetness. Reproducible Python scripts calculate the Mann–Kendall trend test, Sen’s slope, and autocorrelation diagnostics. The primary classification uses a two-sided Mann–Kendall test with the Hamed–Rao variance correction and a significance level of 0.05. Alternative lag configurations are included as sensitivity diagnostics. The game displays these prepared results and charts without performing scientific calculations during play. Learning progresses through four indicative university levels: • First semester: understand the variable, units, study period, and the comparison between the p-value and 0.05. • Third semester: interpret the time series and distinguish statistical significance, trend direction, and magnitude. • Fifth semester: examine temporal autocorrelation and understand why a corrected test is used. • Seventh semester: evaluate data provenance, methodological assumptions, seasonality, and the limits of the conclusions. Every round offers “Significant” and “Non significant” as alternatives. Incorrect answers receive feedback and can be retried. The same two datasets are reused across the levels to deepen understanding. Advanced explanations can be assessed through classroom discussion. Both cases show statistically significant upward trends under the selected analysis. These findings describe the selected episode. The short record and unresolved seasonality limit inference about long-term climate change, causation, or flooding at individual locations. The prototype was developed with Godot and GDScript. Python, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and Matplotlib support data processing and visualization. Statistical results were cross-checked against pyMannKendall. Deliverables include a Windows executable, editable game project, an eleven-page manual, complete datasets, eight scientific charts, and reproducible scripts. The project’s creative contribution is its progression from simple concepts to evidence-based scientific judgment. Its intended impact is to make NASA Earth science data more approachable and support critical interpretation in university education.
